name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q01 - Ancient Indian scientists and their chemical texts

questiontext.text:
Match the ancient Indian scholars/texts with their corresponding contributions to chemistry:

Set 1 (Scholar / Text)Set 2 (Contribution)
(A) Nagarjuna(i) Author of Vaiseshika Sutras and concept of Paramānu
(B) Chakrapani(ii) Author of Rasratnakar on mercury compounds
(C) Acharya Kanda(iii) Encyclopaedia Brihat Samhita on wall coatings and perfumes
(D) Varāhmihir(iv) Discovered mercury sulphide and invented soap

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ancient Indian scientific literature contains extensive records of metallurgy, alchemy, medicine, and early atomic philosophy.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Nagarjuna was a renowned Indian chemist, alchemist, and metallurgist whose work Rasratnakar deals with the formulation of mercury compounds and extraction of metals.
- Chakrapani discovered mercury sulphide and is credited with inventing soap using mustard oil and alkalies.
- Acharya Kanda (originally known as Kashyap) authored Vaiseshika Sutras and proposed the theory of indivisible particles called Paramānu.
- Varāhmihir composed the sixth-century encyclopaedia Brihat Samhita, which describes glutinous wall materials, perfumes, and cosmetics.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Nagarjuna with Rasratnakar; Chakrapani with mercury sulphide and soap; Acharya Kanda with Vaiseshika Sutras and Paramānu; and Varāhmihir with Brihat Samhita.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q02 - Base physical quantities and SI units

questiontext.text:
Match each base physical quantity with its correct SI unit:

Physical QuantitySI Unit
(A) Electric current(i) \(\mathrm{cd}\)
(B) Thermodynamic temperature(ii) \(\mathrm{mol}\)
(C) Amount of substance(iii) \(\mathrm{A}\)
(D) Luminous intensity(iv) \(\mathrm{K}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The International System of Units (SI) defines seven fundamental base physical quantities and their corresponding base units.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Electric current (symbol \(I\)) has the SI unit ampere (\(\mathrm{A}\)).
- Thermodynamic temperature (symbol \(T\)) has the SI unit kelvin (\(\mathrm{K}\)).
- Amount of substance (symbol \(n\)) has the SI unit mole (\(\mathrm{mol}\)).
- Luminous intensity (symbol \(I_v\)) has the SI unit candela (\(\mathrm{cd}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Electric current with \(\mathrm{A}\); Thermodynamic temperature with \(\mathrm{K}\); Amount of substance with \(\mathrm{mol}\); and Luminous intensity with \(\mathrm{cd}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q03 - SI prefixes and their numerical multiples

questiontext.text:
Match the SI prefixes with their respective power-of-ten multiples:

SI PrefixMultiple
(A) micro (\(\mu\))(i) \(10^{9}\)
(B) deca (\(\mathrm{da}\))(ii) \(10^{-15}\)
(C) giga (\(\mathrm{G}\))(iii) \(10^{-6}\)
(D) femto (\(\mathrm{f}\))(iv) \(10^{1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The SI system uses standard prefixes to represent decimal multiples and submultiples of base and derived units.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- The prefix micro (\(\mu\)) represents \(10^{-6}\).
- The prefix deca (\(\mathrm{da}\)) represents \(10^{1}\) (or \(10\)).
- The prefix giga (\(\mathrm{G}\)) represents \(10^{9}\).
- The prefix femto (\(\mathrm{f}\)) represents \(10^{-15}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: micro with \(10^{-6}\); deca with \(10^{1}\); giga with \(10^{9}\); and femto with \(10^{-15}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q04 - Chemical compounds and their societal applications

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical substances with their significance in healthcare or environmental chemistry:

SubstanceRole / Significance
(A) Cisplatin(i) Management of greenhouse gas emissions
(B) AZT (Azidothymidine)(ii) Effective drug in cancer therapy
(C) Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)(iii) Used for helping AIDS patients
(D) Methane (\(\mathrm{CH_4}\))(iv) Responsible for ozone depletion in the stratosphere

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chemistry plays a vital role in synthesising life-saving pharmaceuticals and addressing environmental challenges such as ozone depletion and global warming.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Cisplatin (along with taxol) is a well-known drug effective in cancer therapy.
- AZT (Azidothymidine) is used for helping AIDS patients.
- CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) are environmentally hazardous refrigerants responsible for ozone depletion in the stratosphere.
- Methane (along with carbon dioxide) is a major greenhouse gas whose management is a key environmental concern.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Cisplatin with cancer therapy; AZT with helping AIDS patients; CFCs with stratospheric ozone depletion; and Methane with greenhouse gas management.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q05 - Scientists and laws of chemical combination

questiontext.text:
Match each scientist with the law of chemical combination they proposed:

ScientistLaw Proposed
(A) Antoine Lavoisier(i) Law of Multiple Proportions
(B) Joseph Proust(ii) Law of Conservation of Mass
(C) John Dalton(iii) Law of Gaseous Volumes
(D) Gay-Lussac(iv) Law of Definite Proportions

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Five foundational laws govern the combination of elements to form compounds, each established through careful quantitative experiments in the 18th and early 19th centuries.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Antoine Lavoisier (1789) established the Law of Conservation of Mass from combustion studies.
- Joseph Proust formulated the Law of Definite Proportions using natural and synthetic samples of cupric carbonate.
- John Dalton (1803) proposed the Law of Multiple Proportions.
- Gay-Lussac (1808) observed the Law of Gaseous Volumes for reacting gases at identical temperature and pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Antoine Lavoisier with the Law of Conservation of Mass; Joseph Proust with the Law of Definite Proportions; John Dalton with the Law of Multiple Proportions; and Gay-Lussac with the Law of Gaseous Volumes.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q06 - Macroscopic classification of common substances

questiontext.text:
Match each substance with its correct macroscopic classification:

SubstanceClassification
(A) Air(i) Compound
(B) Mixture of salt and sugar(ii) Element
(C) Silver(iii) Homogeneous mixture
(D) Glucose(iv) Heterogeneous mixture

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At the macroscopic level, matter is classified into mixtures (homogeneous or heterogeneous) and pure substances (elements or compounds).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Air consists of gases completely mixed together with uniform composition throughout, making it a homogeneous mixture.
- A dry mixture of salt and sugar does not have uniform composition throughout and its components remain distinct, making it a heterogeneous mixture.
- Silver consists of only one type of atom, so it is an element.
- Glucose contains carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen combined in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Air with homogeneous mixture; Mixture of salt and sugar with heterogeneous mixture; Silver with element; and Glucose with compound.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q07 - Determining significant figures in numerical values

questiontext.text:
Match each numerical value with its correct number of significant figures:

NumberNumber of Significant Figures
(A) \(0.0025\)(i) \(4\)
(B) \(208\)(ii) \(6\)
(C) \(5005\)(iii) \(2\)
(D) \(126.000\)(iv) \(3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four numerical values are given: \(0.0025\), \(208\), \(5005\), and \(126.000\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard rules for counting significant figures in experimental measurements are applied.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. All non-zero digits are significant.
2. Zeros preceding the first non-zero digit are not significant.
3. Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant.
4. Zeros at the end or right of a number are significant provided they are on the right side of the decimal point.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- In \(0.0025\), the three leading zeros are not significant; only \(2\) and \(5\) are significant, giving \(2\) significant figures.
- In \(208\), the zero lies between non-zero digits \(2\) and \(8\), giving \(3\) significant figures.
- In \(5005\), both zeros lie between non-zero digits, giving \(4\) significant figures.
- In \(126.000\), all three trailing zeros are to the right of the decimal point, giving \(6\) significant figures.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(0.0025\) with \(2\); \(208\) with \(3\); \(5005\) with \(4\); and \(126.000\) with \(6\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q08 - Rounding numbers to three significant figures

questiontext.text:
Match each number with its value correctly rounded off to three significant figures:

Original NumberRounded to 3 Significant Figures
(A) \(34.216\)(i) \(0.0460\)
(B) \(10.4107\)(ii) \(2810\)
(C) \(0.04597\)(iii) \(34.2\)
(D) \(2808\)(iv) \(10.4\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four numbers to be rounded to three significant figures: \(34.216\), \(10.4107\), \(0.04597\), and \(2808\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard rounding rules apply: if the first digit removed is less than \(5\), the preceding digit stays unchanged; if it is greater than \(5\), the preceding digit increases by \(1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Leading zeros in decimal numbers do not count as significant figures, whereas trailing zeros after a decimal point do count.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(34.216\): the fourth significant digit is \(1 < 5\), so it rounds to \(34.2\).
- For \(10.4107\): the fourth significant digit is \(1 < 5\), so it rounds to \(10.4\).
- For \(0.04597\): the first three significant digits are \(4, 5, 9\), and the next digit is \(7 > 5\). Increasing \(9\) by \(1\) carries over to give \(0.0460\) (which has \(3\) significant figures).
- For \(2808\): the fourth digit is \(8 > 5\), so \(0\) increases to \(1\), giving \(2810\) (where the trailing zero without a decimal point is not significant, leaving \(3\) significant figures).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(34.216\) with \(34.2\); \(10.4107\) with \(10.4\); \(0.04597\) with \(0.0460\); and \(2808\) with \(2810\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q09 - Expressing decimal numbers in scientific notation

questiontext.text:
Match each number with its correct scientific notation representation:

Decimal FormScientific Notation
(A) \(0.0048\)(i) \(8.008 \times 10^{3}\)
(B) \(234.000\)(ii) \(5.000 \times 10^{2}\)
(C) \(8008\)(iii) \(4.8 \times 10^{-3}\)
(D) \(500.0\)(iv) \(2.34000 \times 10^{2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four decimal numbers: \(0.0048\), \(234.000\), \(8008\), and \(500.0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In scientific notation \(N \times 10^n\), the digit term \(N\) lies between \(1.000\dots\) and \(9.999\dots\), and all significant figures from the original number are preserved.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Moving the decimal point to the left by \(k\) places gives exponent \(n = +k\); moving it to the right by \(k\) places gives exponent \(n = -k\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(0.0048\): move decimal \(3\) places right \(\rightarrow 4.8 \times 10^{-3}\).
- \(234.000\): move decimal \(2\) places left (preserving all \(6\) significant figures) \(\rightarrow 2.34000 \times 10^{2}\).
- \(8008\): move decimal \(3\) places left \(\rightarrow 8.008 \times 10^{3}\).
- \(500.0\): move decimal \(2\) places left (preserving all \(4\) significant figures) \(\rightarrow 5.000 \times 10^{2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(0.0048\) with \(4.8 \times 10^{-3}\); \(234.000\) with \(2.34000 \times 10^{2}\); \(8008\) with \(8.008 \times 10^{3}\); and \(500.0\) with \(5.000 \times 10^{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q10 - Molecular and formula masses of common substances

questiontext.text:
Match each chemical substance with its molar mass (atomic masses: \(\mathrm{H} = 1.008\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{C} = 12.011\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{O} = 16.00\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{Na} = 23.0\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = 35.5\text{ u}\)):

SubstanceMolar Mass (\(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))
(A) \(\mathrm{CH_4}\)(i) \(58.5\)
(B) \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)(ii) \(180.162\)
(C) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)(iii) \(16.043\)
(D) \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)(iv) \(18.02\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic masses: \(\mathrm{H} = 1.008\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{C} = 12.011\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{O} = 16.00\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{Na} = 23.0\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = 35.5\text{ u}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The molar mass in \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is numerically equal to the molecular or formula mass in \(\mathrm{u}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Molecular/formula mass is the sum of atomic masses of all atoms present in the formula unit or molecule.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{CH_4}\): \(12.011 + 4(1.008) = 16.043\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
- \(\mathrm{H_2O}\): \(2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.016 \approx 18.02\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
- \(\mathrm{NaCl}\): \(23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
- \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\): \(6(12.011) + 12(1.008) + 6(16.00) = 72.066 + 12.096 + 96.00 = 180.162\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) with \(16.043\); \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) with \(18.02\); \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) with \(58.5\); and \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\) with \(180.162\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q11 - Concentration terms and their mathematical definitions

questiontext.text:
Match each solution concentration term with its defining mathematical expression:

Concentration TermMathematical Expression
(A) Mass per cent(i) \(\dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\)
(B) Mole fraction of A(ii) \(\dfrac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\)
(C) Molarity (\(M\))(iii) \(\dfrac{\text{Mass of solute}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\)
(D) Molality (\(m\))(iv) \(\dfrac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{n_{\mathrm{A}} + n_{\mathrm{B}}}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The concentration of a solution expresses the relative amount of solute present in a given quantity of solution or solvent.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Mass per cent is defined as \(\frac{\text{Mass of solute}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\).
- Mole fraction of component A in a binary mixture of A and B is \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{n_{\mathrm{A}} + n_{\mathrm{B}}}\).
- Molarity (\(M\)) is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution.
- Molality (\(m\)) is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Mass per cent with \(\frac{\text{Mass of solute}}{\text{Mass of solution}} \times 100\); Mole fraction of A with \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{A}}}{n_{\mathrm{A}} + n_{\mathrm{B}}}\); Molarity with \(\frac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Volume of solution in litres}}\); and Molality with \(\frac{\text{No. of moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of solvent in kg}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q12 - Calculating number of atoms in different samples

questiontext.text:
Match each sample with the number of atoms present in it (atomic mass of \(\mathrm{He} = 4\text{ u}\), \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\)):

SampleNumber of Atoms
(A) \(52\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Ar}\)(i) \(13\)
(B) \(52\text{ u}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\)(ii) \(7.829 \times 10^{24}\)
(C) \(52\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\)(iii) \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\)
(D) \(12\text{ g}\) of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\)(iv) \(3.131 \times 10^{25}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Samples: \(52\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Ar}\), \(52\text{ u}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\), \(52\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\), and \(12\text{ g}\) of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\). Atomic mass of \(\mathrm{He} = 4\text{ u}\) (molar mass \(= 4\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)); molar mass of \(^{12}\mathrm{C} = 12\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(\mathrm{Ar}\) and \(\mathrm{He}\) are monoatomic noble gases; \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of atoms \(= \text{moles} \times N_A = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{molar mass (g mol}^{-1}\text{)}} \times N_A\). For mass in \(\mathrm{u}\), number of atoms \(= \frac{\text{total mass (u)}}{\text{atomic mass (u)}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(52\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Ar}\): \(52 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.131 \times 10^{25}\) atoms.
- For \(52\text{ u}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\): \(\frac{52\text{ u}}{4\text{ u/atom}} = 13\) atoms.
- For \(52\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\): \(\frac{52\text{ g}}{4\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 13 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 7.829 \times 10^{24}\) atoms.
- For \(12\text{ g}\) of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\): \(\frac{12\text{ g}}{12\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(52\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Ar}\) with \(3.131 \times 10^{25}\); \(52\text{ u}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\) with \(13\); \(52\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\) with \(7.829 \times 10^{24}\); and \(12\text{ g}\) of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\) with \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q13 - Identifying limiting reagents in reaction mixtures

questiontext.text:
Match each reaction mixture with the limiting reagent present in it:

Reaction MixtureLimiting Reagent
(A) \(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 3\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\) in \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB_2}\)(i) \(\mathrm{H_2}\)
(B) \(5\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 2.5\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\) in \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB_2}\)(ii) No limiting reagent
(C) \(100\text{ atoms }\mathrm{A} + 100\text{ molecules }\mathrm{B_2}\) in \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB_2}\)(iii) \(\mathrm{A}\)
(D) \(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{N_2} + 2\text{ mol }\mathrm{H_2}\) in \(\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}\)(iv) \(\mathrm{B_2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three mixtures follow \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{AB_2}\) (\(1:1\) molar/particle ratio), and one mixture follows \(\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}\) (\(1:3\) molar ratio).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely consumed first based on stoichiometric ratios.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Compare available reactant amounts against the stoichiometric ratio required by the balanced chemical equation.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 3\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\): \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{A}\) needs \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2}\); \(\mathrm{B_2}\) is in excess, so \(\mathrm{A}\) is the limiting reagent.
- For \(5\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 2.5\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\): \(2.5\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2}\) needs \(2.5\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{A}\); \(\mathrm{A}\) is in excess, so \(\mathrm{B_2}\) is the limiting reagent.
- For \(100\text{ atoms }\mathrm{A} + 100\text{ molecules }\mathrm{B_2}\): both reactants are present in the exact \(1:1\) stoichiometric ratio, so there is no limiting reagent.
- For \(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{N_2} + 2\text{ mol }\mathrm{H_2}\): \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) requires \(3\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\), but only \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is present, so \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is the limiting reagent.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(2\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 3\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\) with \(\mathrm{A}\); \(5\text{ mol }\mathrm{A} + 2.5\text{ mol }\mathrm{B_2}\) with \(\mathrm{B_2}\); \(100\text{ atoms }\mathrm{A} + 100\text{ molecules }\mathrm{B_2}\) with no limiting reagent; and \(1\text{ mol }\mathrm{N_2} + 2\text{ mol }\mathrm{H_2}\) with \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q14 - Calculating concentrations of aqueous solutions

questiontext.text:
Match each aqueous solution with its calculated concentration value:

Solution DescriptionConcentration
(A) \(4\text{ g}\ \mathrm{NaOH}\) (\(M = 40\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) in \(250\text{ mL}\) solution(i) \(2.79\text{ m}\)
(B) \(20\text{ g}\ \mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\) (\(M = 342\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) in \(2\text{ L}\) solution(ii) \(10\%\text{ (w/w)}\)
(C) \(3\text{ M}\ \mathrm{NaCl}\) (\(M = 58.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) with density \(1.25\text{ g mL}^{-1}\)(iii) \(0.4\text{ M}\)
(D) \(2\text{ g}\) solute dissolved in \(18\text{ g}\) water(iv) \(0.029\text{ M}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four solution compositions are given with their respective solute masses, molar masses, volumes, or densities.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard definitions of molarity (\(M\)), molality (\(m\)), and mass per cent (\(w/w\%\)) apply.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution in L}}}\); \(m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solvent in kg}}}\); \(\text{Mass \%} = \frac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}} \times 100\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(4\text{ g}\ \mathrm{NaOH}\) in \(250\text{ mL}\) (\(0.250\text{ L}\)): \(n = \frac{4}{40} = 0.1\text{ mol}\); \(M = \frac{0.1}{0.250} = 0.4\text{ M}\).
- For \(20\text{ g}\ \mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\) in \(2\text{ L}\): \(n = \frac{20}{342} = 0.0585\text{ mol}\); \(M = \frac{0.0585}{2} \approx 0.029\text{ M}\).
- For \(3\text{ M}\ \mathrm{NaCl}\) with density \(1.25\text{ g mL}^{-1}\): in \(1\text{ L}\) solution, mass of solution \(= 1000 \times 1.25 = 1250\text{ g}\); mass of \(\mathrm{NaCl} = 3 \times 58.5 = 175.5\text{ g}\); mass of water \(= 1250 - 175.5 = 1074.5\text{ g} = 1.0745\text{ kg}\); \(m = \frac{3}{1.0745} = 2.79\text{ m}\).
- For \(2\text{ g}\) solute in \(18\text{ g}\) water: mass of solution \(= 2 + 18 = 20\text{ g}\); mass per cent \(= \frac{2}{20} \times 100 = 10\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(4\text{ g}\ \mathrm{NaOH}\) in \(250\text{ mL}\) with \(0.4\text{ M}\); \(20\text{ g}\) sugar in \(2\text{ L}\) with \(0.029\text{ M}\); \(3\text{ M}\ \mathrm{NaCl}\) with \(2.79\text{ m}\); and \(2\text{ g}\) solute in \(18\text{ g}\) water with \(10\%\text{ (w/w)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q15 - Percentage composition and empirical formulas

questiontext.text:
Match each composition or compound with its corresponding percentage composition or empirical formula (atomic masses: \(\mathrm{H} = 1.008\), \(\mathrm{C} = 12.01\), \(\mathrm{O} = 16.00\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = 35.45\), \(\mathrm{Fe} = 55.85\)):

Compound / Elemental DataComposition / Empirical Formula
(A) \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)(i) \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\)
(C) \(69.9\%\ \mathrm{Fe},\ 30.1\%\ \mathrm{O}\) by mass(iii) \(11.18\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 88.79\%\ \mathrm{O}\)
(D) \(24.27\%\ \mathrm{C},\ 4.07\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 71.65\%\ \mathrm{Cl}\) by mass(iv) \(52.14\%\ \mathrm{C},\ 13.13\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 34.73\%\ \mathrm{O}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two known molecular formulas (\(\mathrm{H_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)) and two sets of elemental mass-percentage data are given.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For empirical formula calculations, a \(100\text{ g}\) sample of the compound is assumed.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Mass \% of element} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol compound}}{\text{molar mass of compound}} \times 100\). Empirical formula is obtained from the simplest whole-number mole ratio of constituent atoms.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) (\(M = 18.02\text{ g}\)): \(\%\mathrm{H} = \frac{2.016}{18.02} \times 100 = 11.18\%\); \(\%\mathrm{O} = \frac{16.00}{18.02} \times 100 = 88.79\%\).
- For \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\) (\(M = 46.068\text{ g}\)): \(\%\mathrm{C} = \frac{24.02}{46.068} \times 100 = 52.14\%\); \(\%\mathrm{H} = \frac{6.048}{46.068} \times 100 = 13.13\%\); \(\%\mathrm{O} = \frac{16.00}{46.068} \times 100 = 34.73\%\).
- For \(69.9\%\ \mathrm{Fe}, 30.1\%\ \mathrm{O}\): \(n_{\mathrm{Fe}} = \frac{69.9}{55.85} = 1.25\), \(n_{\mathrm{O}} = \frac{30.1}{16.00} = 1.88\); ratio \(\mathrm{Fe}:\mathrm{O} = 1 : 1.5 = 2 : 3\), giving \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\).
- For \(24.27\%\ \mathrm{C}, 4.07\%\ \mathrm{H}, 71.65\%\ \mathrm{Cl}\): \(n_{\mathrm{C}} = \frac{24.27}{12.01} = 2.021\), \(n_{\mathrm{H}} = \frac{4.07}{1.008} = 4.04\), \(n_{\mathrm{Cl}} = \frac{71.65}{35.45} = 2.021\); ratio \(\mathrm{C}:\mathrm{H}:\mathrm{Cl} = 1:2:1\), giving \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) with \(11.18\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 88.79\%\ \mathrm{O}\); \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\) with \(52.14\%\ \mathrm{C},\ 13.13\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 34.73\%\ \mathrm{O}\); \(69.9\%\ \mathrm{Fe},\ 30.1\%\ \mathrm{O}\) with \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\); and \(24.27\%\ \mathrm{C},\ 4.07\%\ \mathrm{H},\ 71.65\%\ \mathrm{Cl}\) with \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MATCH_LIST_Q16 - Stoichiometric amounts in chemical reactions

questiontext.text:
Match each chemical reaction condition with the corresponding stoichiometric result:

Reaction ConditionStoichiometric Result
(A) Mass of \(\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\) produced by burning \(16\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CH_4(g)}\) in excess \(\mathrm{O_2}\)(i) \(0.5\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{CH_4}\)
(B) Moles of \(\mathrm{CH_4(g)}\) required to produce \(22\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\)(ii) \(22\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}\)
(C) Mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) (\(M = 100\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) reacting with \(25\text{ mL}\) of \(0.75\text{ M}\ \mathrm{HCl}\)(iii) \(36\text{ g}\ \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(D) Mass of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) produced when \(1\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{C}\) is burnt in \(16\text{ g}\ \mathrm{O_2}\)(iv) \(0.9375\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CaCO_3}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four stoichiometric problems involving combustion of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), combustion of carbon in limited \(\mathrm{O_2}\), and reaction of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) with \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All reactions go to completion according to their balanced chemical equations; molar masses used are \(\mathrm{CH_4} = 16\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 18\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2} = 44\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 100\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. \(\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + 2\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)
2. \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl_2(aq)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)
3. \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Burning \(16\text{ g}\) (\(1\text{ mol}\)) of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) yields \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2O} = 2 \times 18\text{ g} = 36\text{ g}\).
- Producing \(22\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(\frac{22}{44} = 0.5\text{ mol}\)) requires \(0.5\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\).
- \(25\text{ mL}\) of \(0.75\text{ M}\ \mathrm{HCl}\) contains \(0.025 \times 0.75 = 0.01875\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{HCl}\). Since \(2\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{HCl}\) reacts with \(1\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{CaCO_3}\), moles of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3} = \frac{0.01875}{2} = 0.009375\text{ mol}\), which has mass \(0.009375 \times 100 = 0.9375\text{ g}\).
- Burning \(1\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{C}\) in \(16\text{ g}\) (\(0.5\text{ mol}\)) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is limited by \(\mathrm{O_2}\), producing \(0.5\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{CO_2} = 0.5 \times 44 = 22\text{ g}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are: burning \(16\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CH_4}\) with \(36\text{ g}\ \mathrm{H_2O}\); producing \(22\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}\) with \(0.5\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{CH_4}\); \(25\text{ mL}\) of \(0.75\text{ M}\ \mathrm{HCl}\) with \(0.9375\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CaCO_3}\); and \(1\text{ mol}\ \mathrm{C}\) in \(16\text{ g}\ \mathrm{O_2}\) with \(22\text{ g}\ \mathrm{CO_2}\).
